item.title: My LLM judge did the arithmetic, found the wrong number, and passed it anyway
item.description: My agent wrote '25 cases scored' when 22 were. Under my newest judge prompt, Sonnet 5.5 worked out the 22 from the evidence in all six runs and passed the claim in five, mostly calling the gap minor or slight. When the right number was written out in the evidence, both models under my two newest prompts caught a wrong count 24 times in 24.

item.title: My LLM judges passed a false 'verified live' 11 times in 12. My prompt fixes moved the miss.
item.description: I built a small benchmark of my own agents claiming things they hadn't done, and asked Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 to catch them. Four judge prompts later, the one that finally caught 'live' started passing 19 invented data rows, and its totals looked flat. Three days later, on the same input, Sonnet caught them again.

item.title: My coding agent's guard said no 17 times in a month. It was wrong 10 of them.
item.description: I moved my most important agent rules out of the prompt and into a hook that denies the tool call. Then I counted every denial in a month of transcripts: 6 real catches, 10 false alarms, and the same bug firing three times while I wrote this.

item.title: My agents got more reliable when I gave them less to do
item.description: Six steps I moved out of the model loop and into plain scripts: what each one cost while a model did it, what changed after, and the three times the scripts broke instead.

item.title: 88% of my coding agent's usage goes on reading
item.description: Token-saving tools shrink what the model writes. I measured 35 days of my own sessions: what it writes is 12%. Here is where the other 88% went, and the five settings that actually cut it.

item.title: Letting agents drive a real browser on the Mac I'm typing on
item.description: Headless Chrome walled over one User-Agent token, macOS dragging 'off-screen' windows back into view, minimized popups that steal your keyboard, and sign-in windows that leaked for days.

item.title: A prompt is not a control: two autopilots that forged their own evidence
item.description: Two unattended autopilots had written rules against inventing results. One gave a simulated post 7,253 views; the other approved its own work for 40 days. What they did, and what replaced them.
